    Sub-Riemannian geoemtry

    Sub-Riemannian manifolds

    Let \(M^{m+k}\) be a \((m+k)\)-dimensional smooth manifold and \(\mathcal{H}^m\) be a subbundle of \(TM\) of rank \(m\). Assume that \(\mathcal{H}\) satisfies step-\(r\) bracket generating condition for some \(r \geq 1\). This means that, at each point \( x \in M \), the sections of \( \mathcal{H} \), along with all their Lie brackets up to order \( r \), generate the tangent space \( T_xM \). Then the triple \((M^{m+k},\mathcal{H}^m,g_{\mathcal{H}})\) is called a sub-Riemannian manifold, where \(g_{\mathcal{H}}\) is a fiberwise metric on \(\mathcal{H}\). The subbundle \(\mathcal{H}\) is also called the horizontal distribution. Note that one can easily extend \(g_{\mathcal{H}}\) to a Riemannian metric \(g\) on \(TM\) (see, e.g., [Don21]). Throughout the paper, we fix such a metric \(g\) such that \(g|_{\mathcal{H}}=g_{\mathcal{H}}\) and denote the corresponding sub-Riemannian manifold by \((M^{m+k},\mathcal{H}^{m},g)\). The term ``complete'' as it applies to \((M, \mathcal{H}, g)\) will refer to the Riemannian metric \(g\) being complete. Now \(TM\) admits a direct sum decomposition

    \[ TM=\mathcal{H} \oplus \mathcal{V}, \]

    where \( \mathcal{V} \) denotes the vertical distribution, namely the orthogonal complement of \( \mathcal{H} \) with respect to the metric \( g \).
    Then we have the natural projections

    \[ \pi _{\mathcal{H}}:TM \to \mathcal{H}, \quad \pi _{\mathcal{V}}:TM \to \mathcal{V}.\]

    We denote by \(\mathfrak{X},\mathfrak{X}_{\mathcal{H}},\mathfrak{X}_{\mathcal{V}}\) the spaces of all smooth sections of \(TM\), \(\mathcal{H}\) and \(\mathcal{V}\), respectively.

    When dealing with \(L^p\)-vanishing results on sub-Riemannian manifolds, the notion of generalized Sobolev spaces introduced by Rothschild and Stein [RS76] is useful. Let \((M^{m+k},\mathcal{H}^m,g)\) be a sub-Riemannian manifold, and \(U \subset M\) be a coordinate neighborhood on which a horizontal frame \(\{e_1,\dots,e_m\}\) is defined. The generalized Sobolev spaces is defined as

    \[ S_{l}^{p}(U)=\left\{ u \in L^p(U)|e_{i_1} \cdots e_{i_s}(u) \in L^p(U), 1 \leq i_{1} \leq \cdots \leq i_s \leq m, 0 \leq s \leq l \right\}. \]

    These notions can be easily extended to any relatively compact domain.

    Next, we recall some examples of sub-Riemannian manifolds.

    Example (Riemannian foliations)

    Let \((M^{m+k},\mathcal{F}^k)\) be a foliated manifold, where \(\mathcal{F}^k\) is a \(k\)-dimensional foliation. Let \(g\) be a Riemannian metric on \(M\) and decompose the tangent bundle

    \[ TM=T\mathcal{F} \oplus \mathcal{H} \]

    accordingly, where \(\mathcal{H}\) is complementary to \(T\mathcal{F} \). The metric \(g\) is said to be bundle-like if the Lie derivate of \(g_{\mathcal{H}}\) along vertical direction vanishes. Geometrically, this condition implies that the foliation arises locally from a Riemannian submersion.
    The triple \((M^{m+k},\mathcal{F}^k,g)\) is referred to as a Riemannian foliation, see [CDHL26] or [GW09] for more details. When \(\mathcal{H}\) is bracket generating, \((M^{m+k},\mathcal{H}^m,g)\) is a sub-Riemannian manifold.

    Carnot groups are typical examples in sub-Riemannian geometry. Moreover, they can be endowed with a bundle-like metric structure, see [Bau26].

    Example (Carnot groups)

    \label{exCar} A Carnot group is a simply connected Lie group \(G\) whose Lie algebra \(\mathfrak{g}\) admits a stratified decomposition:

    \[ \mathfrak{g}=V_1 \oplus V_2 \oplus \cdots \oplus V_r \quad (r \geq 1) \]

    such that \([V_1,V_j]=V_{j+1}\) for \(1 \leq j \leq r-1\) and \([V_1,V_r]=\{0\}\). This gives a Lie algebra grading

    \begin{equation}\label{31} [V_i,V_j] \subset V_{i+j}, \end{equation}

    where \(V_j:=\{0\}\) for \(j >r\). Define a distribution \(\mathcal{H}\) on \(G\) by

    \[ \mathcal{H}_x=dL_{x}(V_1) \subset T_xG, \quad \forall x \in G .\]

    Here \(L_x\) is the left translation of \(G\) relative to \(x\).
    Let \(g_{\mathcal{H}}\) be a left-invariant metric on \(\mathcal{H}\). We can extend \(g_{\mathcal{H}}\) to a Riemannian metric \(g\) such that \(V_i \perp V_j\) for \(i \neq j\). Then \((G,\mathcal{H},g)\) is a step-\(r\) sub-Riemannian manifold. Thus we have decomposition:

    \[ TG=\mathcal{H} \oplus \mathcal{V} .\]

    Since \([\mathcal{V}, \mathcal{V}] \subset \mathcal{V}\), \(\mathcal{V}\) is the vertical bundle of a foliation \(\mathcal{F}\) on \(G\).

    Example (Contact manifolds, cf. [Bla10])

    \label{excont} Let \(M^{2m+1}\) be a contact manifold with structure tensors \(( \phi , \mathsf{T} , \theta , g)\). Precisely speaking, \(\theta \) is a contact form (i.e., \(\theta \wedge (d \theta)^m \neq 0\)), \(\mathsf{T}\) is the Reeb vector field, \(\phi \) is a \((1,1)\)-tensor and \(g\) is a Riemannian metric such that

    \begin{equation}\label{2} \begin{cases} \phi ^2=-I+\theta \otimes \mathsf{T}, \quad \phi (\mathsf{T})=0, \quad \theta (\mathsf{T})=1; &\text{}\\ g(\phi X,\phi Y) = g(X,Y)-\theta (X)\theta (Y), &\text{} \forall X,Y \in TM;\\ g(X,\phi Y)=d \theta (X,Y),&\text{} \forall X,Y \in TM. \end{cases} \end{equation}

    The vertical and horizontal distributions are given by \(\mathcal{V}:=\Span_{\rr} \{\mathsf{T}\} \) and \(\mathcal{H}:=\ker \theta \). It follows from the last equality of \eqref{2} that \(\mathcal{H}\) is step-\(2\) bracket generating, hence \((M^{2m+1},\mathcal{H}^{2m},g)\) is a sub-Riemannian manifold.

    Example (Pseudo-Hermitian manifolds)

    Let \(M\) be a real \((2m+p)\)-dimensional oriented manifold. A CR structure of type \((m,p)\) is a complex subbundle \(H^{1,0}\) of \(TM \otimes \cc\), of complex rank \(m\), satisfying the (formally) integrable condition. The pair \((M,H^{1,0})\) is called a CR manifold of type \((m,p)\). Set \(H^{0,1}=\overline{H^{1,0}}\). Alternatively, the CR structure can be described by a pair \((\mathcal{H},J_b)\), where \(\mathcal{H} \) is the real bundle \(\Re\{H^{1,0} \oplus H^{0,1}\}\) and \(J_b\) is its almost complex structure defined by \(J_b(X+\overline{X})=\sqrt{-1}(X-\overline{X})\) for all \(X \in H^{1,0}\).

    Let us consider the special case that \((M,H^{1,0})\) is a CR manifold of type \((m,1)\), which is also referred as hypersurface type (see [DT06, \S 1.1] for details).
    Since \(M\) is oriented, there is a \(1\)-form \(\theta \) which annihilates \(\mathcal{H}\). Define the Levi form \(L_{\theta }\) by

    \[ L_\theta (X,Y)=d \theta (X,J_b Y), \quad \forall X,Y \in \mathfrak{X}_{\mathcal{H}} . \]

    When \(L_\theta \) is positive definite on \(\mathcal{H}\), the CR manifold \((M,H^{1,0})\) is said to be strictly pseudoconvex and the triple \((M^{2m+1},\mathcal{H},\theta )\) is called a pseudo-Hermitian manifold. This also implies that \(\mathcal{H}\) is step-\(2\) bracket generating. Clearly, \(\theta \) is a contact form and there is a unique Reeb vector field \(\mathsf{T} \) satisfying

    \[ \theta (\mathsf{T} )=1, \quad i_{\mathsf{T}}(d \theta) =0. \]

    The collection of all its integral curves forms an oriented one-dimensional foliation \(\mathcal{V}\) on \(M\), which is called the Reeb foliation. Define \(J\) as the extension of \(J_b\) to \(TM\) satisfying \(J(\mathsf{T})=0\). Then there is a canonical metric called Webster metric on \(M\), given by

    \[ g=L_{\theta }+\theta \otimes \theta . \]

    Now \(\mathcal{V}\) is the orthogonal complementary of \(\mathcal{H}\) with respect to \(g\).
    Note that \(g(JX,JY)=g(X,Y)\) for all \(X,Y \in \mathfrak{X}_{\mathcal{H}}\). Obviously, \((M^{2m+1},\mathcal{H},g)\) is a sub-Riemannian manifold. There are two natural connections on a pseudo-Hermitian manifold, the Levi-Civita connection \(\nabla \) and the Tanaka-Webster connection \(\nabla ^{TW}\). It's known that \(\nabla ^{TW}\) is compatible with the CR structure and the metric. The pseudo-Hermitian torsion of \(\nabla ^{TW}\), denoted by \(\tau \), is given by

    \[ \tau (X)=T_{\nabla ^{TW}}(\mathsf{T},X) \]

    for all \(X \in \mathfrak{X}(M)\), where \(T_{\nabla ^{TW}}\) is the torsion tensor of \(\nabla ^{TW}\). The pseudo-Hermitian manifold \((M^{2m+1},\mathcal{H},\theta )\) is called Sasakian if \(\tau =0\).
    For more information about pseudo-Hermitian geometry we refer the reader to [DT06] or [CDRY19].

    In [Bej78], A. Bejancu introduced the notion of CR-submanifolds, which serve as an intermediate class between complex submanifolds and totally real submanifolds in complex differential geometry.

    Example (CR-submanifolds, cf. [Bej86])

    \label{exCrsub} Let \((M,g)\) be a submanifold of a Hermitian manifold \((\widetilde{M},J,\tilde{g})\), where \(g\) is the induced metric on \(M\) from \(\tilde{g}\). The submanifold \(M\) is called a CR-submanifold in \(\widetilde{M}\) if there is a \(C^{\infty}\) distribution \(\mathcal{H}\) on \(M\) satisfying the following conditions: (i) \(J(\mathcal{H}_x)= \mathcal{H}_x\) for each \(x \in M\); (ii) \(J(\mathcal{V}_x) \subset T_{x}^{\perp}M\) for each \(x\in M\), where \(\mathcal{V}\) is the orthogonal complement of \(\mathcal{H}\) in \(TM\) according to \(g\), and \(T^{\perp}M\) is the normal bundle of \(M\) in \(\widetilde{M}\). Let \(2m\) and \(p\) denote the ranks of \(\mathcal{H}\) and \(\mathcal{V}\) respectively. Then it follows from [BC79, Theorem 4.1] that \((M,\mathcal{H},J|_{\mathcal{H}})\) is a CR manifold of type \((m,p)\). We remark, however, that the induced metric \(g\) (in the case \(p=1\)) doesn't coincide with the Webster metric in general. If \(\mathcal{H}\) satisfies bracket generating condition, then \((M,\mathcal{H},g)\) is a sub-Riemannian manifold.

    Bott connection

    It would be convenient to introduce a suitable linear connection compatible with the sub-Riemannian structure on \((M,H,g_H;g)\) in some sense. The generalized Bott connection is one of such connections given by

    \[ \nabla^{\mathfrak B}_X Y = \begin{cases} \pi_H\bigl(D_XY\bigr), & X,Y\in\Gamma(H),\\[4pt] \pi_H\bigl([X,Y]\bigr), & X\in\Gamma(V),\ Y\in\Gamma(H),\\[4pt] \pi_V\bigl([X,Y]\bigr), & X\in\Gamma(H),\ Y\in\Gamma(V),\\[4pt] \pi_V\bigl(D_XY\bigr), & X,Y\in\Gamma(V). \end{cases} \]

    where \(D\) denotes the Riemannian connection of \(g\). Clearly, \(\nabla^{B}\) preserves the decomposition, and it also satisfies

    \[ \nabla^{B}_X g_H=0 \qquad\text{and}\qquad \nabla^{B}_Y g_V=0 \]

    for any \(X\in H\) and \(Y\in V\). However, \(\nabla^{B}\) does not preserve the Riemannian metric \(g\) in general.

    Lemma

    For any \(X,Y\in\Gamma(TM)\), we have

    \[ T^{\nabla ^B}(X,Y) = -\pi_V\bigl([\pi_H(X),\pi_H(Y)]\bigr) -\pi_H\bigl([\pi_V(X),\pi_V(Y)]\bigr). \]

    Hladky connection

    Hladky connection is a generalization of Tanaka-Webster connection.

    Definition

    The Hladky connection \(\nabla \) on a sub-Riemannian manifold \((M,\mathcal{H},g)\) is given by

    \begin{equation}\label{conn6} \nabla _{X}Y= \begin{cases} (D_XY)_{\mathcal{H}} &\text{if } X,Y \in \mathfrak{X} _{\mathcal{H}}\\ ([X,Y])_{\mathcal{H}}+B_{X}Y &\text{if } X \in \mathfrak{X}_{\mathcal{V}},Y \in \mathfrak{X} _{\mathcal{H}}\\ ([X,Y])_{\mathcal{V}} +C_XY&\text{if } X \in \mathfrak{X}_{\mathcal{H}},Y \in \mathfrak{X} _{\mathcal{V}}\\ (D_XY)_{\mathcal{V}} &\text{if } X,Y \in \mathfrak{X} _{\mathcal{V}}, \end{cases} \end{equation}

    where \(D\) is the Levi-Civita connection of \(g\), and tensors \(B\) and \(C\) are defined by

    \[ \la B_{X}Y,Z \ra= \frac{1}{2}(L_{{X_{\mathcal{V}}}}g)(Y_{\mathcal{H}},Z_{\mathcal{H}})\]

    and

    \[ \la C_{X}Y,Z \ra= \frac{1}{2}(L_{{X_{\mathcal{H}}}}g)(Y_{\mathcal{V}},Z_{\mathcal{V}}).\]

    The torsion \(T\) of \(\nabla \) satisfies

    \begin{equation}\label{tor7} T(X,Y)=\begin{cases} -[X,Y]_{\mathcal{V}} &\text{if } X,Y \in \mathfrak{X}_{\mathcal{H}}\\ B_XY-C_YX &\text{if } X \in \mathfrak{X}_{\mathcal{V}},Y \in \mathfrak{X} _{\mathcal{H}}\\ C_XY-B_YX&\text{if } X \in \mathfrak{X}_{\mathcal{H}},Y \in \mathfrak{X} _{\mathcal{V}}\\ -[X,Y]_{\mathcal{H}} &\text{if } X,Y \in \mathfrak{X}_{\mathcal{V}} \end{cases} \end{equation}

    Actually, Hladky gives the following characterization of \(\nabla \).

    Proposition (cf. [Hla2012])

    There exists a unique metric connection \(\nabla\) on \(M\) such that: \begin{itemize} \item \(\mathcal H\) and \(\mathcal V\) are \(\nabla\)-parallel, i.e., for every \(X\in\Gamma(\mathcal H)\), \(Y\in\Gamma(TM)\), and \(Z\in\Gamma(\mathcal V)\),

    \[ \nabla_Y X\in\Gamma(\mathcal H), \qquad \nabla_Y Z\in\Gamma(\mathcal V). \]

    \item The torsion \(T\) of \(\nabla\) satisfies

    \[ T(\mathcal H,\mathcal H)\subset \mathcal V, \qquad T(\mathcal V,\mathcal V)\subset \mathcal H. \]

    \item For every \(X,Y\in\Gamma(\mathcal H)\) and \(V,Z\in\Gamma(\mathcal V)\),

    \[ \langle T(X,Z),Y\rangle = \langle T(Y,Z),X\rangle, \qquad \langle T(Z,X),V\rangle = \langle T(V,X),Z\rangle. \]

    \end{itemize}

    Remark

    Note that Hladky connection \(\nabla \) and Levi-Civita connection \(D\) are related by

    \begin{equation}\label{027} \nabla_X Y=D_X Y+\frac{1}{2} T(X, Y)-\frac{1}{2} J_X Y-\frac{1}{2} J_Y X, \quad X, Y \in \mathfrak{X}( M) . \end{equation}

    See also [Bau26]. Here \(J\) is defined by

    \[ \la J_Z X, Y \ra = \la Z, T(X,Y) \ra, \quad \forall X, Y,Z \in \mathfrak{X}( M).\]

    Since the Hladky connection is metric, \(\nabla g=0\), differentiating gives

    \[ \left\langle (\nabla_W J)_Z X, Y \right\rangle = \left\langle Z, (\nabla_W T)(X,Y) \right\rangle \quad \forall X, Y,Z,W \in \mathfrak{X}( M). \]

    Setting

    \begin{equation}\label{A1} A_XY:= -\frac{1}{2} T(X, Y)+\frac{1}{2} J_X Y+\frac{1}{2} J_Y X, \quad X, Y \in \mathfrak{X}( M), \end{equation}

    which implies

    \begin{equation}\label{A2} A_{\mathcal{H}}\mathcal{H} \subset \mathcal{V},\quad A_{\mathcal{V}}\mathcal{V} \subset \mathcal{H}. \end{equation}

    Then \(D=\nabla +A\), and

    \begin{equation}\label{Dnab} \begin{aligned} R^g(X, Y )Z=& R(X,Y)Z+ (\nabla _XA)_{Y}Z-(\nabla _YA)_XZ\\ &+A_{T(X,Y)}Z+A_X A_Y Z-A_Y A_X Z . \end{aligned} \end{equation}

    Having introduced the basic notions associated with the Hladky connection, we next recall some important classes of sub-Riemannian manifolds that provide natural geometric settings.

    Example (Riemannian foliations)

    Let \((M^{m+k},\mathcal{F}^k)\) be a foliated manifold, where \(\mathcal{F}^k\) is a \(k\)-dimensional foliation. Let \(g\) be a Riemannian metric on \(M\) and decompose the tangent bundle

    \[ TM=T\mathcal{F} \oplus \mathcal{H} \]

    accordingly, where \(\mathcal{H}\) is complementary to \(T\mathcal{F} \). The metric \(g\) is said to be bundle-like if the Lie derivate of \(g_{\mathcal{H}}\) along vertical direction vanishes. Geometrically, this condition implies that the foliation arises locally from a Riemannian submersion.
    The triple \((M^{m+k},\mathcal{F}^k,g)\) is referred to as a Riemannian foliation, see [CDHL26] or [GW09] for more details. When \(\mathcal{H}\) is bracket generating, \((M^{m+k},\mathcal{H}^m,g)\) is a sub-Riemannian manifold.

    Definition (cf. [Bau2022Htype])

    Let \((M^{m+k},\mathcal{H}^m,g)\) be a Riemannian foliation. If its leaves are totally geodesic, then \((M^{m+k},\mathcal{H}^m,g)\) is called a totally geodesic foliation.

    Proposition

    Let \((M^{m+k},\mathcal{H}^m,g)\) be a Riemannian foliation. Then it's a totally geodesic foliation if and only if

    \[ C=0. \]

    Proof

    For \(Y,Z \in \mathfrak{X}_{\mathcal{V}}\) and \(X \in \mathfrak{X}_{\mathcal{H}}\), we have

    \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} 2\la C_{X}Y,Z \ra=& X \la Y,Z \ra -\la [X,Y],Z \ra-\la Y,[X,Z ]\ra\\ =& \la \nabla _Y X ,Z \ra +\la Y ,\nabla _Z X\ra\\ =&- \la \nabla _Y Z+\nabla _Z Y,X \ra. \end{aligned} \end{equation}

    The integrability of \(\mathcal{V}\) implies

    \[ \begin{aligned} - \la \nabla _Y Z+\nabla _Z Y,X \ra=& - \la 2\nabla _Y Z+[Z, Y],X \ra\\ =& - \la 2\nabla _Y Z,X \ra, \end{aligned} \]

    from which the conclusion follows.

    Remark

    If \((M^{m+k},\mathcal{H}^m,g)\) is a Riemannian foliation with totally geodesic leaves, then the Hladky connection coincides with the generalized Bott connection.

    sub-Riemannian manifold with transverse symmetries

    In this section, we introduce Baudoin-Garofalo's [BauGar2017trsy] notion of a sub-Riemannian manifold with transverse symmetries is a particularly structured way of adding “vertical directions” to a sub-Riemannian manifold.

    Start with a sub-Riemannian manifold \( (M,\mathcal H,g_{\mathcal H}), \) where \(\mathcal H\subset TM\) is bracket generating. A vector field \(Z\) is called a sub-Riemannian Killing field if its flow preserves both the horizontal distribution and the horizontal metric. Concretely,

    \[ [Z,X]\in \Gamma(\mathcal H) \quad\text{for every }X\in\Gamma(\mathcal H), \]

    and

    \[ (\mathcal L_Z g_{\mathcal H})(X,Y)=0, \qquad X,Y\in\Gamma(\mathcal H). \]

    Thus flowing in the \(Z\)-direction does not change the sub-Riemannian geometry.

    The key assumption is that there exists a finite-dimensional Lie algebra \(\mathcal V\) of such symmetries satisfying

    \[ \boxed{ T_xM=\mathcal H_x\oplus\mathcal V_x \qquad \text{for every }x\in M. } \]

    The directions generated by \(\mathcal V\) are called the vertical directions. So the tangent bundle splits into horizontal directions, where the sub-Riemannian metric lives, and vertical directions which act as infinitesimal symmetries of that geometry.

    This is why the term transverse symmetries is appropriate: the vertical vector fields are transverse to \(\mathcal H\), and their flows preserve \((\mathcal H,g_{\mathcal H})\).

    If one chooses an inner product on \(\mathcal V\), one obtains a Riemannian extension

    \[ g=g_{\mathcal H}\oplus g_{\mathcal V}. \]

    But Baudoin-Garofalo emphasize that the important geometric objects they construct ultimately do not depend on this auxiliary choice.

    There is also a canonical connection \(\nabla\), characterized by

    \[ \begin{aligned} &\nabla g=0,\\ &\nabla_XY\in\mathcal H \qquad (X,Y\in\mathcal H),\\ &\nabla Z=0 \qquad (Z\in\mathcal V), \end{aligned} \]

    and

    \[ T(X,Y)\in\mathcal V,\qquad T(X,Z)=0. \]

    More explicitly,

    \[ \nabla_XY=\pi_{\mathcal H}(D_XY),\qquad \nabla_ZX=[Z,X],\qquad \nabla Z=0, \]

    where \(D\) is the Levi-Civita connection of the chosen Riemannian extension.

    So the torsion on horizontal vectors is essentially the obstruction to integrability of \(\mathcal H\):

    \[ T(X,Y)=-\pi_{\mathcal V}[X,Y]. \]

    This should look very familiar from Hladky and Bott setting.

    A useful geometric picture is that, when the Lie group generated by \(\mathcal V\) acts properly, one has a quotient

    \[ M\longrightarrow M/\mathbb V, \]

    which becomes a Riemannian submersion after choosing the vertical metric. Baudoin–Garofalo mention the Hopf fibration

    \[ S^3\to S^2 \]

    as a basic example.

    The class is quite broad. Their examples include:

    \[ \text{Sasakian manifolds},\qquad \text{step-two Carnot groups},\qquad \text{certain principal bundles}, \]

    and related homogeneous models.
